editorNote: Spellbooks, cartridge standards and social modems fill the December computer desk.
morningLine: At the Macintosh, a novice magician wins by thinking rather than fighting.

lead.headline: Enchanter brings a spellbook to the Macintosh
lead.dek: Infocom’s adventure rewards ingenuity as a novice confronts the sorcerer Krill.
body: An adventure need not begin with a drawn sword. In Infocom’s Enchanter, the Circle of Enchanters sends a novice to confront the sorcerer Krill. Marc Berman’s December COMPUTE! review follows that journey on the Macintosh, where words and spells supply the action.

Scrolls teach spells that change objects and allow communication with animals. The challenge is to discover what a magical tool can do and when to use it. Berman stresses that outwitting opponents is more effective than killing them: the keyboard becomes an instrument of deduction rather than reflex.

The review praises the adventure’s continuity, challenge and documentation, while finding some humor and writing less successful. That mixed verdict makes Enchanter more than a holiday advertisement. Its appeal rests on the sustained pleasure of solving a world whose rules must be learned.

On the Macintosh, Berman reports a 122K game and a further 139K system folder. A saved game takes 13K; he estimates room for ten saves on the game disk. Apple II, Atari and Commodore 64 disk versions are also listed. This is December review coverage, not an announcement of a new release during December 17–23.

stories.headline: MSX promises a common language for home computers
body: More than a dozen electronics and computer makers are preparing inexpensive MSX machines for an anticipated American entry in early 1985, according to December’s COMPUTE! report. Microsoft developed and licensed the standard; Kazuhiko Kaye Nishi is identified as a driving force. The January Las Vegas electronics show is an expected showcase, not a completed launch.

The proposition is practical: cartridges and standards-compliant peripherals should work across brands. Sony, Yamaha, Sanyo and other licensees could offer different cabinets without making each owner start a separate software library. The reported specification includes a Z80A processor, TI 9918A video, 16 colors, 32 programmable sprites and three-channel sound.

Whether mature 8-bit hardware can compete with newer machines remains the question. The magazine projects low-end prices around $200 or less, rather than quoting an American retail offer. Software breadth and mass marketing may count as much as processor novelty.

stories.headline: Plus/4 improves BASIC but leaves C64 software behind
body: John J. Anderson’s December Creative Computing column finds promise and problems in Commodore’s Plus/4. Its 64K memory leaves about 60K for BASIC, and more than 75 commands broaden the language. Built-in applications cover word processing, spreadsheets and file management, alongside a machine-language monitor.

The buyer’s difficulty is compatibility. C64 software does not carry over, and joystick, cassette and cartridge connections differ. Anderson criticizes the bundled applications and expects a premium over the C64. A familiar Commodore name does not mean a familiar software shelf.

Graphics include a 320-by-200 bitmap mode, but no hardware sprites. Anderson’s wished-for compatible C128 is an editorial proposal, not an announced shipping product. His separate discussion of the Amiga Lorraine concerns a prototype acquired earlier, not a new machine launched this week.

stories.headline: A modem makes the home computer social
body: COMPUTE! opens its Telecomputing Today column this month with Arlan R. Levitan, an AMIS bulletin-board software designer and CompuServe assistant sysop. His subject is the people at the other end of the telephone line, not simply another solitary program.

CompuServe’s CB simulation offers conversation; The Source’s POST helps connect buyers and collectors; Delphi’s ORACLE brings questions to self-described experts. Free public bulletin boards and public-domain terminal programs provide other entrances. Levitan reports that reliable modems can cost under $100, without identifying a particular offer here.

The economics are not uniformly attractive. Levitan contrasts electronic newspaper costs of $5 to $10 with a 25-cent printed paper and describes slow adoption of electronic banking. Yet conversation and shared interests give the home computer a purpose that a new spreadsheet alone cannot supply.

computerItems.title: Amiga Lorraine prototype
computerItems.summary: Anderson reports Commodore acquired the project earlier; prototype described as 8 MHz 68000, three custom chips for graphics/sound/I/O, 128K expandable to at least 1 MB, four-channel stereo and a 5.25-inch 320K internal floppy. market.headline: The software library is part of the purchase
market.summary: MSX promises inter-brand cartridge compatibility, while Plus/4 buyers cannot carry over C64 software. The price of a new box is only one part of changing systems. MSX’s projected US prices are not current retail quotations.

worldAnchor.headline: Britain and China agree Hong Kong’s future
worldAnchor.summary: Britain and China sign the Joint Declaration on December 19. It sets July 1, 1997 for China’s resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong and promises a special administrative region with high autonomy except in foreign and defence affairs, with stated policies unchanged for 50 years.

curiosity.headline: A television with an MSX hiding below the picture
curiosity.summary: General’s Japanese television contains a built-in home computer.
curiosity.detail: COMPUTE!’s December MSX report describes a 14-inch General Corporation TV with its tuner and MSX computer behind a three-inch panel below the screen; attach a detachable keyboard to use it as a computer. Cartridge and printer connections are integral. Reported Japanese price converts to about $550; not a US offer or a December-week launch.
